nameStory: The Cornish bellflower gets its name from its bell-shaped white flowers that dangle like tiny church bells. Despite the "Cornish" in its name, this plant isn't actually from Cornwall, England – it's native to the mountains of Turkey and the Caucasus region. The name likely stuck because it became popular in English gardens, including those in Cornwall.
description: Cornish bellflower is a clump-forming perennial that creates neat mounds of fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves. It grows 12-24 inches tall and spreads up to 18 inches wide, making it a perfect size for garden borders. The most striking feature is its pure white, tubular bell-shaped flowers that hang gracefully from upright stems. This is primarily a garden plant in New England, originally from mountainous regions far from here.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white, tubular bell-shaped flowers about an inch long with pointed petal tips that flare outward. They hang downward from the stems like tiny white church bells.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped basal leaves about 3 inches long with toothed edges and a distinctly fuzzy, grayish texture that feels soft and slightly velvety to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, vigorous clumps that spread outward, staying compact at 12-24 inches tall but gradually expanding to 18 inches wide.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy quality due to fine hairs covering the leaves and stems, giving it a grayish-green appearance.

habitat: In New England, Cornish bellflower is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, particularly perennial borders and rock gardens. With only one recorded observation in our region, it's extremely rare in the wild. When grown here, it prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New heart-shaped leaves emerge with their characteristic fuzzy, grayish texture, forming fresh clumps as the plant begins its growing season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the distinctive white bell-shaped flowers hang from upright stems, creating the plant's most identifiable feature.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules may form, while the fuzzy basal leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground parts visible until spring growth resumes.

funFact: Despite being called "Cornish" bellflower, this plant has traveled an incredible journey – from the high mountains of Turkey and the Caucasus, through European gardens, and finally to New England, where it's so rare that it's been spotted only once in the entire region!
confusionNotes: Other white-flowered bellflowers like Peach-leaved Bellflower have more upright, cup-shaped flowers, while Cornish bellflower's bells hang downward. The fuzzy, grayish heart-shaped leaves are unique among bellflowers – most others have smooth, green foliage.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "alliariifolia" means "leaves like Alliaria" (garlic mustard), referring to the heart-shaped, toothed leaf structure. This is primarily an ornamental escape rather than a naturalized wildflower in New England.
compareHints: Among New England's bellflowers, Cornish bellflower stands out with its fuzzy, grayish leaves and pure white hanging bells. Common Harebell has much smaller, blue flowers and thin leaves, while Creeping Bellflower has purple flowers and smooth green foliage. The heart-shaped, velvety-textured basal leaves are unlike any other bellflower in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the delicate common harebell with its slender nodding flowers, creeping bellflower is much taller and more robust with larger, more substantial bell-shaped blooms.
Intermediate bellflower sits between common harebell (which is smaller and more delicate) and the larger, showier bellflowers like giant bellflower.

Unlike the more common creeping bellflower which has rougher, heart-shaped leaves and smaller purple flowers, peach-leaved bellflower has distinctively glossy, narrow leaves and much larger cup-shaped blooms.
Unlike the small, delicate bells of common harebell or the upright flower clusters of creeping bellflower, spotted bellflower has distinctly large, pendant flowers with internal spotting.

Unlike its bellflower relatives, clustered bellflower has flowers packed into tight, dense clusters rather than scattered along the stem like creeping bellflower or dangling singly like common harebell.
Among New England's bellflowers, Nettle-leaved Bellflower is distinguished by its robust size and those distinctively serrated, nettle-like leaves.
Unlike its relative the common harebell which grows tall and loose in meadows, Giesecke's harebell stays extremely low and compact as an adaptation to fierce mountain winds.
Unlike the more common creeping bellflower which grows upright and has true bell-shaped flowers, trailing bellflower stays low to the ground with star-shaped blooms.

Common harebell is much more delicate and slender than its bellflower relatives like creeping bellflower or clustered bellflower, which tend to be more robust plants with upward-facing or clustered flowers.

Canterbury bells stand out among their bellflower relatives primarily due to their impressive size - both the individual flowers and overall plant are much larger than species like common harebell or creeping bellflower.
Giant Bellflower stands out from other New England bellflowers by its impressive size and distinctly broad, heart-shaped leaves.
